title: Show the Signal, Hide the Noise:Spectral Forcing for Pixel-Space Diffusion

paper.title: Show the Signal, Hide the Noise: Spectral Forcing for Pixel-Space Diffusion
paper.abstract: Abstract Pixel-space diffusion models are trained on full-bandwidth noisy images, yet the useful signal available to the denoiser is strongly frequency dependent. Under rectified-flow diffusion and natural-image power-law spectra, the per-band data-to-noise contour k ∗ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α k^{\ast}(t)=(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} separates a signal-bearing low-frequency region from a noise-dominated high-frequency region at each time t t . We show that this implicit coarse-to-fine structure is not merely descriptive: it induces a capacity-allocation problem. A standard pixel-space denoiser must discover the moving bandwidth boundary internally and can spend computation on frequency-time regions where the optimal prediction collapses to deterministic baselines rather than data-distribution modeling. To make this boundary explicit, we introduce Spectral Forcing , a parameter-free, time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass operator applied to the noisy input before the patch embedder. Its cutoff expands monotonically with the diffusion time and becomes the identity at the data endpoint. Through controlled synthetic experiments, we identify the regime in which the operator is beneficial: coarse patch tokenization and data whose high-frequency content is predominantly noise rather than essential signal. On ImageNet-256 with JiT-700M/32, Spectral Forcing consistently improves both FID and Inception Score across different training epochs, demonstrating robust gains throughout training; at finer tokenization, the spectral forcing is still competitive. We further insert the unchanged operator into SenseNova-U1, a unified text-to-image model, where it improves DPG-Bench and GenEval, showing that the input-side spectral prior transfers beyond class-conditional generation. These results suggest a route to capacity-efficient pixel-space diffusion by showing the signal and hiding the noise.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Spectral Forcing for pixel-space diffusion. Left: the per-band data-to-noise contour k ∗ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α k^{\ast}(t){=}(1{-}t)^{-2/\alpha} separates a signal-bearing region (data-distribution work) from a noise-dominated region where an unforced denoiser collapses to a closed-form map (wasted capacity). Right: SF imposes the boundary explicitly with a parameter-free, time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass at cutoff c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) , applied before the patch embedder; c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) grows monotonically with t t and is the identity at t = 1 t{=}1 . Bottom strip: one operator step — noisy input → \to 2D-DCT → \to mask above c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) → \to IDCT → \to denoiser ε θ \varepsilon_{\theta} . The diffusion objective, architecture, and sampler are unchanged. Diffusion and flow-based models are the state of the art for generating high-quality images. Until recently, the dominant recipe was to operate in a compressed latent space produced by a separately trained autoencoder, with the diffusion model itself learning to denoise latents rather than pixels. This separation has been justified on practical grounds (latents are smaller and faster to denoise), but it adds an external dependency to the generative recipe and obscures the spectral structure of the underlying images. Recent work shows that pixel-space diffusion can be competitive when the architecture is properly designed, in particular through coarse patch tokenization and large transformer backbones [ 24 , 32 , 50 ] . A common observation across these recipes is that diffusion training is implicitly coarse-to-fine: at each timestep the noise level determines a frequency band above which the data signal is buried in noise, and the network must learn to reconstruct lower-frequency content first and higher-frequency content last [ 18 ] . This implicit hierarchy has been documented through frequency-content analyses but has rarely been exploited as an explicit architectural prior. We argue that the hierarchy is not merely descriptive but induces a capacity-allocation problem: a standard pixel-space denoiser, faced with the full bandwidth of the noisy input at every timestep, must discover the moving bandwidth boundary internally and can spend computation on frequency-time regions where the optimal prediction collapses to deterministic baselines rather than data-distribution modeling. The reason this hierarchy emerges is straightforward. Under rectified-flow diffusion, the network at time t t observes z t = t ​ x + ( 1 − t ) ​ ε z_{t}=t\,x+(1-t)\,\varepsilon with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) . For natural-image-like data with power spectrum P ⁡ ( k ) ∝ k − α P(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} , the per-band data-to-noise ratio is k − α / ( 1 − t ) 2 k^{-\alpha}/(1-t)^{2} (the data spectrum compared to the additive-noise variance floor; see Section 3.1 for the relation to the standard z t z_{t} -SNR), and the contour DNR ⁡ ( k , t ) = 1 \mathrm{DNR}(k,t)=1 defines a moving cutoff k ∗ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α k_{*}(t)=(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} that separates a signal-bearing region from a noise-dominated region ( Fig. 1 , left). The standard network has no architectural awareness of this cutoff: it must identify it implicitly from the noise schedule, and allocate capacity between learning data-distribution structure where signal exists and reproducing deterministic baselines where it does not. We confirm this allocation directly with a per-band MSE diagnostic at convergence on synthetic data ( Section 3.2 ): the network does meaningful data-distribution work only in a wedge of ( t , k ) (t,k) space, and converges to deterministic baselines elsewhere. We ask: can making the bandwidth boundary explicit at the input free model capacity for the harder part of the task? We introduce Spectral Forcing ( SF ), a parameter-free time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass mask applied to the network input before the patch embedder ( Fig. 1 , right). The mask’s cutoff radius c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) grows monotonically with the diffusion timestep along a fixed-by-design schedule that is imposed at the input rather than estimated from the data spectrum, restricting the network’s view of z t z_{t} to the bands where signal can dominate, and saturating to the identity at the data endpoint so the trajectory still integrates full-bandwidth velocity. The operator introduces no learnable parameters, costs about half a percent of total compute at 256 2 256^{2} , and composes with any pixel-space rectified-flow recipe without modifying the forward process, the loss, the EMA, the sampler, or classifier-free guidance. SF is regime-dependent. We show, both in toys and on ImageNet, that the operator delivers its largest gains in a specific conjunction of conditions: (i) the model’s patch tokenization is coarse enough that the patchify already aggressively bandlimits the representation, and (ii) the data’s high-frequency content is predominantly noise rather than essential signal. When these conditions hold, the operator delivers consistent improvements throughout training; when they do not, it remains competitive with the unforced baseline. We make this regime explicit through a controlled toy experiment so that practitioners know where to expect headline gains versus where the operator’s main role is as a non-harmful regularizer. The coarse-tokenization regime is also the operating point of recent native vision-language models [ 7 ] that bypass an external visual encoder and process raw image patches directly, where token count must be kept small for tractable joint sequence modelling; making capacity-efficient pixel-space diffusion practical in this regime is therefore a downstream-relevant target. On ImageNet-256 the empirical headline is sharp. At the JiT-700M/32 configuration (64 transformer tokens, the largest configuration in Li and He [24] ), SF reduces FID from 24.19 24.19 to 20.68 20.68 ( + 14 % +14\% ) and improves Inception Score from 83.28 83.28 to 93.96 93.96 ( + 13 % +13\% ) in an apples-to-apples 60-epoch comparison against a same-recipe baseline. The improvement is robust across training budgets: SF consistently improves both FID and Inception Score at every epoch checkpoint we evaluate, demonstrating that the gain is not a transient data-efficiency artifact. At finer tokenization (256 tokens, JiT-130M/16), SF remains competitive with the baseline at the matched 60-epoch budget, delimiting the regime where it produces additional headline gains versus where it serves as a non-harmful frequency prior. Our work makes the following contributions: • We formalize a per-band data-to-noise analysis as a closed-form bandwidth-coherence framework that predicts the operator’s optimal cutoff schedule, the analytical bandwidth front c ( t ) ∝ ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α c(t)\propto(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} , and identifies its regime of applicability. • We design a controlled 1D-to-2D toy experiment that derives the operator from a per-band MSE diagnostic (showing that an unforced network has converged to a deterministic baseline outside a wedge of ( t , k ) (t,k) space), characterizes its dependence on patch size and data spectrum, and exposes when it helps or hurts. We verify the same wedge structure directly on real ImageNet checkpoints. • We validate on ImageNet-256: a + 14.5 % +14.5\% FID and + 13 % +13\% Inception Score gain at JiT-700M/32 in an apples-to-apples 60 60 -epoch comparison, holding + 8.0 % +8.0\% at 120 120 epochs where SF already matches a published ∼ \sim 145 145 -epoch reference. Our method surpasses constant low-pass, spatial Gaussian blur, Focal Frequency Loss [ 20 ] , blurring diffusion [ 17 ] , and DCTDiff [ 32 ] at the same operating point. Together these results suggest a simple route to more capacity-efficient pixel-space diffusion by showing the denoiser the signal and hiding the noise.

sections.heading: Diffusion and pixel-space generation.
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-matching dominate high-quality image generation [ 44 , 13 , 31 , 45 , 46 , 21 , 26 , 27 , 1 ] , typically with transformer backbones [ 9 , 33 , 28 ] replacing U-Nets [ 38 ] . Latent diffusion compresses images via separately trained autoencoders [ 37 , 34 , 10 , 23 ] , with recent work substituting representation-rich tokenizers for faster convergence [ 54 , 52 , 56 , 41 , 55 , 12 ] . Pixel-space diffusion is the alternative [ 6 , 40 , 30 , 14 , 16 , 4 , 50 , 25 , 29 ] ; we build on JiT [ 24 ] , where large-patch transformers match latent baselines without auxiliary losses. The coarse-tokenization regime is also the operating point of native VLMs [ 7 ] that process raw image patches without a separate encoder. SF is a parameter-free input-side adapter that composes with any of these and leaves forward process, loss, and sampler unchanged.

sections.heading: Spectral and frequency-domain methods.
sections.text: Some prior work makes the forward process itself spectral, replacing Gaussian noise with progressive blurring or wavelet shrinkage [ 36 , 17 ] ; analyses without modifying the forward process formalize standard diffusion’s implicit coarse-to-fine character [ 18 ] and link it to the spectral bias of neural networks [ 35 , 47 , 42 ] and natural-image power-law statistics [ 49 , 3 , 39 ] . Other work generates directly in a frequency representation [ 32 ] or coarse-to-fine token order [ 19 , 51 , 48 , 5 , 11 , 53 , 43 ] , sometimes with frequency-aware objectives [ 20 , 22 ] . Latent Forcing [ 2 ] cascades a frozen semantic encoder with a pixel-level diffusion head. SF differs structurally: the forward process is unchanged rectified-flow, the architecture is unchanged, and the operator is a parameter-free time-conditional mask on the pixel input whose schedule is derived from the per-band data-to-noise contour of the unmodified forward process.

sections.text: The bandwidth front k ∗ ​ ( t ) k_{*}(t) partitions the ( k , t ) (k,t) plane into signal-bearing (below) and noise-dominated (above) regions; as t → 1 t\to 1 the front sweeps outward, exposing more bands. The empirical question is whether a standard pixel-space denoiser uses this structure, and where the allocation becomes wasteful. We answer with three controlled experiments on small models ( Fig. 2 ), before any version of Spectral Forcing is introduced: a 1D rectified-flow Transformer ( ∼ 178 {\sim}178 k params) on synthetic 1D power-law signals, and a 2D DiT ( ∼ 3 {\sim}3 M params) on h × h h{\times}h synthetic images at h = 64 h{=}64 , trained under the recipe of Eq. 3 . sections.heading: Schedule shape and time-dependence.
sections.text: Time-dependence is forced by the data endpoint. A constant low-pass with c < 1 c<1 cannot reach the natural-image distribution because it permanently zeros bands the data does have, leaving excess high-frequency mass in any generated sample. A constant c = 1 c=1 is the no-op. The interesting design space is therefore the family of monotonic f ⁡ ( t ) f(t) that interpolate between an aggressive cutoff at t = 0 t=0 and the identity at t = 1 t=1 . sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Spectral Forcing turns the bandwidth boundary that diffusion training discovers implicitly into an explicit input-side prior: a parameter-free time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass applied before the patch embedder, with a cutoff schedule derived from the per-band data-to-noise contour of the unmodified rectified-flow process. The operator composes with any pixel-space recipe at negligible compute overhead. At JiT-700M/32 on ImageNet-256 it delivers improvements in both FID and Inception Score, and reaches the previously published reference in substantially fewer epochs; at finer tokenization the operator is neither helpful nor harmful, which delimits its applicability cleanly. The coarse tokenization paired with noise-dominated high-frequency content, coincides with the operating point at which pixel-space transformers and native vision-language models are practical.

sections.heading: Appendix A Implementation Details
sections.text: Our implementation closely follows the JiT recipe of Li and He [24] , with Spectral Forcing as a deterministic input-side adapter applied before the patch embedder. The configurations of all our experiments are summarized in Table 9 ; we describe the details below.

sections.heading: Time distribution.
sections.text: Following Esser et al. [10] , during training we adopt a logit-normal distribution over t t : logit ⁡ ( t ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , σ 2 ) \mathrm{logit}(t)\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) . We sample s ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , σ 2 ) s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) and let t = sigmoid ⁡ ( s ) t=\mathrm{sigmoid}(s) . The hyper-parameter μ \mu shifts the typical noise level; following Li and He [24] we use μ = − 0.8 \mu=-0.8 and σ = 0.8 \sigma=0.8 on ImageNet-256 throughout.

sections.heading: Backbone and patchify.
sections.text: We use the JiT architecture of Li and He [24] unmodified, at three configurations: JiT-130M/32 (64 transformer tokens at 256 2 256^{2} ), JiT-130M/16 (256 tokens), and JiT-700M/32 (64 tokens, the largest configuration in Li and He [24] ). The DCT window in the SF operator is matched to the patch size in the patch embedder.

sections.heading: Spectral Forcing operator.
sections.text: The operator applies a single soft 2D-DCT radial low-pass to the full rectified-flow input z t ∈ ℝ C × H × W z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} before the patch embedder; the DCT is taken over the whole H × W H\times W grid, so the radial cutoff acts on global image frequencies. Its hyper-parameters are the cutoff end-points c min , c max ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{\min},c_{\max}\in[0,1] , the schedule shape f ⁡ ( t ) f(t) , and the soft-mask sharpness κ \kappa in σ ⁡ ( κ ⁡ ( c ⁡ ( t ) − r ⁡ ( u , v ) ) ) \sigma\!\big(\kappa(c(t)-r(u,v))\big) ; the analytical schedule additionally uses the spectrum exponent α \alpha . Throughout the paper we fix c min = 0.05 c_{\min}=0.05 , c max = 1.0 c_{\max}=1.0 , and κ = 30 \kappa=30 , and use the linear schedule f ⁡ ( t ) = t f(t)=t unless otherwise noted (the analytical schedule f ( t ) ∝ ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α f(t)\propto(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} is used only in the toy resolution-scaling experiments).

sections.heading: Toy experiments.
sections.text: The 1D rectified-flow Transformer used in Section 3.2 has ∼ 178 \sim 178 k parameters (4 layers, 200 epochs); the 2D DiT used in Section 5 has ∼ 3 \sim 3 M parameters and is trained on synthetic h × h h\times h -pixel images with h ∈ { 64,128,256,512 } h\in\{64,128,256,512\} , batch size 64, AdamW with learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} . Multi-seed runs use n ∈ { 3 , 4 , 5 } n\in\{3,4,5\} depending on resolution; ranges are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation throughout.

sections.heading: ImageNet effective α \alpha .
sections.text: The bandwidth-coherence framework uses the effective power-law exponent α \alpha of the natural-image radial DCT spectrum. We center-crop and resize a sample of N = 200 N=200 ImageNet-256 images, apply the 2D DCT-II per channel, average power per radial bin (32 bins), and fit log ⁡ P ⁡ ( k ) = b ​ log ⁡ k + c \log P(k)=b\log k+c over bins 1 through 31 (skipping DC and the saturated tail). The result is slope b = − 2.818 b=-2.818 , so the effective α = 2.82 \alpha=2.82 over three decades of clean linear fit.

sections.heading: B.5 Closed-form denoising limit.
sections.text: With the rectified-flow interpolant z t = t ​ x + ( 1 − t ) ​ ε z_{t}=t\,x+(1-t)\,\varepsilon , ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , the per-sample velocity target is exactly v target = x − z t 1 − t = x − ε . v_{\text{target}}\;=\;\frac{x-z_{t}}{1-t}\;=\;x-\varepsilon. (9) Reasoning per radial band k k , write z t , k = t ​ x k + ( 1 − t ) ​ ε k z_{t,k}=t\,x_{k}+(1-t)\,\varepsilon_{k} with ε k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \varepsilon_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) and x k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , P ⁡ ( k ) ) x_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P(k)) , P ⁡ ( k ) ∝ k − α P(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} . The two contributions to z t , k z_{t,k} have typical magnitudes t ​ P ⁡ ( k ) t\sqrt{P(k)} (signal) and 1 − t 1-t (noise); the closed-form denoising corner is the high- k k region where the band is noise-dominated, t ​ P ⁡ ( k ) ≪ 1 − t t\sqrt{P(k)}\ll 1-t , at t t bounded away from 1 1 . There the signal term is negligible against the noise floor, z t , k ≈ ( 1 − t ) ​ ε k z_{t,k}\approx(1-t)\,\varepsilon_{k} , so the noise is recoverable from the input, ε k ≈ z t , k / ( 1 − t ) \varepsilon_{k}\approx z_{t,k}/(1-t) . Substituting into ( 9 ), v target , k = x k − ε k ≈ − ε k ≈ − z t , k 1 − t ⟹ v target ≈ − z t 1 − t . v_{\text{target},k}\;=\;x_{k}-\varepsilon_{k}\;\approx\;-\varepsilon_{k}\;\approx\;-\frac{z_{t,k}}{1-t}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_{\text{target}}\approx-\frac{z_{t}}{1-t}. sections.heading: B.7 Qualitative samples.
sections.text: Fig. 6 shows nine ImageNet classes generated by the same JiT-700M/32 model at 120 120 epochs, comparing the no-mask baseline (FID 16.46 16.46 ) against Linear- SF (FID 15.15 \mathbf{15.15} , + 8.0 % +8.0\% ). Each pair fixes both the class label and the sample index, so the only experimental variable is whether the time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass was active during training and sampling. The classes span birds (lorikeet, indigo bunting), mammals (golden retriever, lion), marine subjects (stingray, coral reef), prepared food (pizza, hot dog), and a structured-scene class (cliff dwelling). Across all nine, SF samples are visibly crisper in fine structure and more class-coherent at this converged budget; the effect is strongest on textured surfaces (lion mane, coral, pizza topping, cliff dwelling stonework) where the no-mask baseline tends to produce smoother but less specific texture.

sections.heading: Per-step compute overhead.
sections.text: SF adds one forward and one inverse 2D-DCT per denoising step — approximately 0.5 % 0.5\% of per-step compute relative to the unmasked baseline at JiT-130M/32, 256 2 256^{2} ( Section 5 ), with no learned parameters and no additional memory. The DCT is parallelizable on the patch grid and runs in the same kernel as patchify; for budgets where 0.5 % 0.5\% matters, the operator is a no-op to remove.

sections.heading: Hyperparameters held fixed across all ImageNet runs.
sections.text: The cutoff bounds ( c min , c max ) = ( 0.05 , 1.0 ) (c_{\min},c_{\max}){=}(0.05,1.0) and the mask sharpness κ = 30 \kappa{=}30 are reused unchanged across every ImageNet configuration in Table 9 , with no per-model, per-budget, or per-resolution tuning. The c min c_{\min} sweep of Section B.1 indicates the operator is not narrowly tuned at this point; per-configuration tuning would only widen the reported gap to baseline.

sections.heading: Single benchmark and architecture family.
sections.text: We report on ImageNet-256, the canonical class-conditional FID/IS benchmark, and on JiT [ 24 ] , a modern pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer. SF is parameter-free and recipe-agnostic by construction, so applying it to other backbones (e.g., DiT, U-Net) or other diffusion forwards is a configuration change, not an algorithmic change.

Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/weepiess2383/Spectral_Forcing . Abstract Pixel-space diffusion models are trained on full-bandwidth noisy images, yet the useful signal available to the denoiser is strongly frequency dependent. Under rectified-flow diffusion and natural-image power-law spectra, the per-band data-to-noise contour k ∗ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α k^{\ast}(t)=(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} separates a signal-bearing low-frequency region from a noise-dominated high-frequency region at each time t t . We show that this implicit coarse-to-fine structure is not merely descriptive: it induces a capacity-allocation problem. A standard pixel-space denoiser must discover the moving bandwidth boundary internally and can spend computation on frequency-time regions where the optimal prediction collapses to deterministic baselines rather than data-distribution modeling. To make this boundary explicit, we introduce Spectral Forcing , a parameter-free, time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass operator applied to the noisy input before the patch embedder. Its cutoff expands monotonically with the diffusion time and becomes the identity at the data endpoint. Through controlled synthetic experiments, we identify the regime in which the operator is beneficial: coarse patch tokenization and data whose high-frequency content is predominantly noise rather than essential signal. On ImageNet-256 with JiT-700M/32, Spectral Forcing consistently improves both FID and Inception Score across different training epochs, demonstrating robust gains throughout training; at finer tokenization, the spectral forcing is still competitive. We further insert the unchanged operator into SenseNova-U1, a unified text-to-image model, where it improves DPG-Bench and GenEval, showing that the input-side spectral prior transfers beyond class-conditional generation. These results suggest a route to capacity-efficient pixel-space diffusion by showing the signal and hiding the noise. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Spectral Forcing for pixel-space diffusion. Left: the per-band data-to-noise contour k ∗ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α k^{\ast}(t){=}(1{-}t)^{-2/\alpha} separates a signal-bearing region (data-distribution work) from a noise-dominated region where an unforced denoiser collapses to a closed-form map (wasted capacity). Right: SF imposes the boundary explicitly with a parameter-free, time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass at cutoff c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) , applied before the patch embedder; c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) grows monotonically with t t and is the identity at t = 1 t{=}1 . Bottom strip: one operator step — noisy input → \to 2D-DCT → \to mask above c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) → \to IDCT → \to denoiser ε θ \varepsilon_{\theta} . The diffusion objective, architecture, and sampler are unchanged. Diffusion and flow-based models are the state of the art for generating high-quality images. Until recently, the dominant recipe was to operate in a compressed latent space produced by a separately trained autoencoder, with the diffusion model itself learning to denoise latents rather than pixels. This separation has been justified on practical grounds (latents are smaller and faster to denoise), but it adds an external dependency to the generative recipe and obscures the spectral structure of the underlying images. Recent work shows that pixel-space diffusion can be competitive when the architecture is properly designed, in particular through coarse patch tokenization and large transformer backbones [ 24 , 32 , 50 ] . A common observation across these recipes is that diffusion training is implicitly coarse-to-fine: at each timestep the noise level determines a frequency band above which the data signal is buried in noise, and the network must learn to reconstruct lower-frequency content first and higher-frequency content last [ 18 ] . This implicit hierarchy has been documented through frequency-content analyses but has rarely been exploited as an explicit architectural prior. We argue that the hierarchy is not merely descriptive but induces a capacity-allocation problem: a standard pixel-space denoiser, faced with the full bandwidth of the noisy input at every timestep, must discover the moving bandwidth boundary internally and can spend computation on frequency-time regions where the optimal prediction collapses to deterministic baselines rather than data-distribution modeling. The reason this hierarchy emerges is straightforward. Under rectified-flow diffusion, the network at time t t observes z t = t ​ x + ( 1 − t ) ​ ε z_{t}=t\,x+(1-t)\,\varepsilon with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) . For natural-image-like data with power spectrum P ⁡ ( k ) ∝ k − α P(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} , the per-band data-to-noise ratio is k − α / ( 1 − t ) 2 k^{-\alpha}/(1-t)^{2} (the data spectrum compared to the additive-noise variance floor; see Section 3.1 for the relation to the standard z t z_{t} -SNR), and the contour DNR ⁡ ( k , t ) = 1 \mathrm{DNR}(k,t)=1 defines a moving cutoff k ∗ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α k_{*}(t)=(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} that separates a signal-bearing region from a noise-dominated region ( Fig. 1 , left). The standard network has no architectural awareness of this cutoff: it must identify it implicitly from the noise schedule, and allocate capacity between learning data-distribution structure where signal exists and reproducing deterministic baselines where it does not. We confirm this allocation directly with a per-band MSE diagnostic at convergence on synthetic data ( Section 3.2 ): the network does meaningful data-distribution work only in a wedge of ( t , k ) (t,k) space, and converges to deterministic baselines elsewhere. We ask: can making the bandwidth boundary explicit at the input free model capacity for the harder part of the task? We introduce Spectral Forcing ( SF ), a parameter-free time-conditional 2D-DCT low-pass mask applied to the network input before the patch embedder ( Fig. 1 , right). The mask’s cutoff radius c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) grows monotonically with the diffusion timestep along a fixed-by-design schedule that is imposed at the input rather than estimated from the data spectrum, restricting the network’s view of z t z_{t} to the bands where signal can dominate, and saturating to the identity at the data endpoint so the trajectory still integrates full-bandwidth velocity. The operator introduces no learnable parameters, costs about half a percent of total compute at 256 2 256^{2} , and composes with any pixel-space rectified-flow recipe without modifying the forward process, the loss, the EMA, the sampler, or classifier-free guidance. SF is regime-dependent. We show, both in toys and on ImageNet, that the operator delivers its largest gains in a specific conjunction of conditions: (i) the model’s patch tokenization is coarse enough that the patchify already aggressively bandlimits the representation, and (ii) the data’s high-frequency content is predominantly noise rather than essential signal. When these conditions hold, the operator delivers consistent improvements throughout training; when they do not, it remains competitive with the unforced baseline. We make this regime explicit through a controlled toy experiment so that practitioners know where to expect headline gains versus where the operator’s main role is as a non-harmful regularizer. The coarse-tokenization regime is also the operating point of recent native vision-language models [ 7 ] that bypass an external visual encoder and process raw image patches directly, where token count must be kept small for tractable joint sequence modelling; making capacity-efficient pixel-space diffusion practical in this regime is therefore a downstream-relevant target. On ImageNet-256 the empirical headline is sharp. At the JiT-700M/32 configuration (64 transformer tokens, the largest configuration in Li and He [24] ), SF reduces FID from 24.19 24.19 to 20.68 20.68 ( + 14 % +14\% ) and improves Inception Score from 83.28 83.28 to 93.96 93.96 ( + 13 % +13\% ) in an apples-to-apples 60-epoch comparison against a same-recipe baseline. The improvement is robust across training budgets: SF consistently improves both FID and Inception Score at every epoch checkpoint we evaluate, demonstrating that the gain is not a transient data-efficiency artifact. At finer tokenization (256 tokens, JiT-130M/16), SF remains competitive with the baseline at the matched 60-epoch budget, delimiting the regime where it produces additional headline gains versus where it serves as a non-harmful frequency prior. Our work makes the following contributions: • We formalize a per-band data-to-noise analysis as a closed-form bandwidth-coherence framework that predicts the operator’s optimal cutoff schedule, the analytical bandwidth front c ( t ) ∝ ( 1 − t ) − 2 / α c(t)\propto(1-t)^{-2/\alpha} , and identifies its regime of applicability. • We design a controlled 1D-to-2D toy experiment that derives the operator from a per-band MSE diagnostic (showing that an unforced network has converged to a deterministic baseline outside a wedge of ( t , k ) (t,k) space), characterizes its dependence on patch size and data spectrum, and exposes when it helps or hurts. We verify the same wedge structure directly on real ImageNet checkpoints. • We validate on ImageNet-256: a + 14.5 % +14.5\% FID and + 13 % +13\% Inception Score gain at JiT-700M/32 in an apples-to-apples 60 60 -epoch comparison, holding + 8.0 % +8.0\% at 120 120 epochs where SF already matches a published ∼ \sim 145 145 -epoch reference. Our method surpasses constant low-pass, spatial Gaussian blur, Focal Frequency Loss [ 20 ] , blurring diffusion [ 17 ] , and DCTDiff [ 32 ] at the same operating point. Together these results suggest a simple route to more capacity-efficient pixel-space diffusion by showing the denoiser the signal and hiding the noise. 2 Related Work Diffusion and pixel-space generation. Diffusion and flow-matching dominate high-quality image generation [ 44 , 13 , 31 , 45 , 46 , 21 , 26 , 27 , 1 ] , typically with transformer backbones [ 9 , 33 , 28 ] replacing U-Nets [ 38 ] . Latent diffusion compresses images via separately trained autoencoders [ 37 , 34 , 10 , 23 ] , with recent work substituting representation-rich tokenizers for faster convergence [ 54 , 52 , 56 , 41 , 55 , 12 ] . Pixel-space diffusion is the alternative [ 6 , 40 , 30 , 14 , 16 , 4 , 50 , 25 , 29 ] ; we build on JiT [ 24 ] , where large-patch transformers match latent baselines without auxiliary losses. The coarse-tokenization regime is also the operating point of native VLMs [ 7 ] that process raw image patches without a separate encoder. SF is a parameter-free input-side adapter that composes with any of these and leaves forward process, loss, and sampler unchanged. Spectral and frequency-domain methods. Some prior work makes the forward process itself spectral, replacing Gaussian noise with progressive blurring or wavelet shrinkage [ 36 , 17 ] ; analyses without modifying the forward process formalize standard diffusion’s implicit coarse-to-fine character [ 18 ] and link it to the spectral bias of neural networks [ 35 , 47 , 42 ] and natural-image power-law statistics [ 49 , 3 , 39 ] . Other work generates directly in a frequency representation [ 32 ] or coarse-to-fine token order [ 19 , 51 , 48 , 5 , 11 , 53 , 43 ] , sometimes with frequency-aware objectives [ 20 , 22 ] . Latent Forcing [ 2 ] cascades a frozen semantic encoder with a pixel-level diffusion head. SF differs structurally: the forward process is unchanged rectified-flow, the architecture is unchanged, and the operator is a parameter-free time-conditional mask on the pixel input whose schedule is derived from the per-band data-to-noise contour of the unmodified forward process. 3 Methodology 3.1 Preliminaries Rectified-flow.
